questions.question: In which part of the kidney are structures W and X on the nephron diagram located (options: cortex, inner medulla, outer medulla, renal pelvis)?
questions.answer: A: cortex
steps: W is the glomerulus inside the Bowman capsule and X is the proximal convoluted tubule.
Both lie in the kidney cortex, so the answer is A; the loop of Henle and collecting duct dip into the medulla.

questions.question: In which labelled structure of the nephron diagram does ultrafiltration take place (options W, X, Y, Z)?
questions.answer: A: W
steps: Ultrafiltration happens where blood in the glomerulus capillaries is under high pressure inside the Bowman capsule.
This is structure W (glomerulus and capsule); X is the proximal tubule (reabsorption), Y the loop of Henle and Z the collecting duct.

questions.question: Which labelled structures on the nephron diagram form part of the loop of Henle (options: X only, X and Y, Y only, Y and Z)?
questions.answer: C: Y only
steps: Y is the long hairpin descending into the medulla, which is the loop of Henle.
X is the proximal convoluted tubule and Z is the collecting duct, which are not part of the loop.

questions.question: Explain how ultrafiltration removes urea from the blood.
questions.answer: Urea is small and dissolved in plasma, so it is forced through the glomerulus capillary walls into Bowman capsule by high pressure.
steps: Blood entering the glomerulus is at high hydrostatic pressure.
Small soluble molecules such as urea pass through the capillary endothelium and basement membrane.
Urea enters the Bowman capsule as part of the glomerular filtrate, then flows into the nephron.
Urea is not reabsorbed in significant amounts, so it leaves the body in urine.

questions.question: Deduce why the kangaroo rat is more successful than the brown rat at living in desert habitats, using the table of kidney adaptations.
questions.answer: The kangaroo rat makes much more concentrated urine, so it loses less water: its thick ascending limb has more mitochondria, so it pumps more Na+ out and builds a steeper concentration gradient in the medulla.
steps: Urine concentration is 5500 mOsmol dm^-3 in the kangaroo rat compared with 2900 in the brown rat, so it loses less water for the same solute excretion.
Its thick ascending limb has more mitochondria (5.5 against 3.6), so more ATP is available for active transport of Na+ and Cl- out of the ascending limb.
Medulla sodium concentration is 95 mmol dm^-3 against 45, so water potential in the medulla is much lower.
A steeper water potential gradient means more water leaves the collecting duct by osmosis and is reabsorbed, which conserves water in a desert.

questions.question: Which component of the nervous system continues a reflex arc immediately after the receptor is stimulated (options: motor neurone, relay neurone, Schwann cell, sensory neurone)?
questions.answer: D sensory neurone
steps: The receptor is stimulated and sends the impulse into the reflex arc.
The next component is the sensory neurone, which carries the impulse to the CNS.
Relay neurones come later in the CNS, and Schwann cells only insulate axons.

questions.question: Which pathway shows a reflex arc (options AW, BX, CY, DZ)?
questions.answer: C: receptor -> spinal cord -> muscle
steps: A reflex arc runs from receptor, along a sensory neurone to the CNS (here the spinal cord), then along a motor neurone to the effector, which is a muscle.
Options A and B start at the muscle, and D skips the receptor and goes through the brain, so only C is a reflex arc.

questions.question: Describe how the resting potential of -70 mV is maintained in the axon when no pressure is applied.
questions.answer: The Na+/K+ pump actively moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in using ATP, and the membrane is more permeable to K+, giving a negative inside.
steps: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na+ out of the axon and 2 K+ into the axon.
This creates a higher concentration of Na+ outside and of K+ inside.
The membrane is more permeable to K+ (K+ leak channels), so K+ diffuses out down its gradient.
K+ leaving with no balancing anion leaves the inside negative, giving the resting potential of about -70 mV.

questions.question: Suggest how a change in pressure at the Pacinian corpuscle causes an action potential in the axon.
questions.answer: Pressure deforms the corpuscle and stretches the axon membrane, opening Na+ channels; Na+ influx depolarises it to threshold.
steps: Pressure on the Pacinian corpuscle deforms its layers.
This stretches the membrane of the sensory neurone at its end, opening stretch-mediated sodium channels.
Na+ diffuses into the axon, making the inside less negative (a generator potential).
If the depolarisation reaches threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and an action potential is generated.

questions.question: Explain why the membrane potential at electrode Y was the same when medium or high pressure was applied to the fingertip.
questions.answer: Once threshold is reached an action potential always has the same size (all-or-nothing); higher pressure only increases the frequency.
steps: Medium and high pressure both produce a generator potential that reaches threshold.
An action potential is all-or-nothing: once threshold is reached it has the same size (about +40 mV).
Higher pressure makes action potentials more frequent rather than bigger.
So the membrane potential measured at Y is the same at medium and high pressure.

questions.question: Describe the role of calcium ions in producing contraction of a muscle fibre.
questions.answer: Ca2+ binds to troponin, moving tropomyosin off the actin binding sites so myosin can form cross bridges.
steps: A nerve impulse releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Ca2+ binds to troponin, which changes shape.
This moves tropomyosin away from the myosin binding sites on actin, so cross bridges can form and the muscle contracts.

questions.question: Explain how the features of slow twitch fibres, shown in the table, benefit an Olympic marathon runner.
questions.answer: Many mitochondria, much myoglobin and a large capillary network allow sustained aerobic respiration, and slow sustained contraction suits long-distance running without fatigue.
steps: Many mitochondria give a high rate of aerobic respiration, producing plenty of ATP for sustained contraction over the whole race.
Many myoglobin molecules store oxygen in the fibre and release it to the mitochondria, so aerobic respiration can continue.
A larger capillary network brings more oxygen and glucose and removes CO2 and lactate, so fatigue is delayed.
Slow, sustained contraction means the muscle can keep working for long periods, which is needed in a marathon.

questions.question: Comment on the rate of heat loss during exercise, using the graph of heat loss at rest and during exercise.
questions.answer: Heat loss rises sharply soon after exercise starts, then levels off at a plateau well above the resting rate (roughly 5 times higher on the graph).
steps: The rate of heat loss is constant at rest, then increases rapidly once exercise starts and slows as it approaches a plateau.
Contracting muscles respire faster and release much more heat, so the body must lose heat faster (more sweating and skin vasodilation) to stop the core temperature rising.
The plateau shows heat loss now matches heat production, so a steady, raised body temperature is maintained (negative feedback).

questions.question: Describe the difference between a negative feedback mechanism and a positive feedback mechanism.
questions.answer: Negative feedback reverses a change to return conditions to a set point; positive feedback amplifies the change further.
steps: Negative feedback: a change triggers a response that opposes and reverses the change, returning conditions to normal (homeostasis).
Positive feedback: a change triggers a response that increases the change further, pushing it away from the set point.
Negative feedback is the common homeostatic control; positive feedback is rarer, for example in blood clotting or childbirth.

questions.question: Which statement about thermoregulation at a body temperature of 37 degrees C is correct (options given in text)?
questions.answer: D the body temperature is maintained in a dynamic equilibrium
steps: Thermoregulation is always required to keep temperature steady.
The body always generates heat and loses heat, so statement B is false.
Heat production and loss are balanced (dynamic equilibrium), so D is correct.

questions.question: Explain how small molecules such as creatinine are filtered from the blood in the glomerulus.
questions.answer: High hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules through the capillary wall and basement membrane into Bowman capsule.
steps: The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, so pressure in the glomerulus is high.
Small molecules such as creatinine can pass through the gaps (fenestrations) in the capillary endothelium.
They then pass through the basement membrane, where larger molecules such as proteins and blood cells are retained.
Podocytes and the filtration slits prevent the filtrate from reaching the cells, so the filtrate contains only small molecules.

questions.question: Calculate the GFR of a person who excreted 1960 mg of creatinine in urine over 15 hours (3 s.f.).
steps: The rate at which creatinine is filtered equals the rate at which it appears in urine, as creatinine is not reabsorbed or secreted.
Rate = amount / time = 1960 / 15 = 130.67 mg h^-1.
To 3 significant figures this is 131 mg h^-1.

questions.question: Comment on the results of the clinical trial of surgery on glucose uptake in the presence of insulin.
questions.answer: Surgery increased glucose uptake in all three groups, with the largest rise in the diabetic groups; after surgery the pre-diabetic and type II means are similar to the non-diabetic mean before surgery, but the large standard deviations overlap.
steps: Mean uptake was higher after surgery in every group: non-diabetic 1.07 to 1.39, pre-diabetic 0.55 to 1.30 and type II 0.40 to 1.10 a.u.
The increase was proportionally biggest in the type II group (0.70 a.u., about 175%) and pre-diabetic group, but only about 30% in the non-diabetic group.
After surgery, pre-diabetic (1.30) and type II (1.10) uptake is close to the non-diabetic value before surgery (1.07), so the body cells respond to insulin better.
However the standard deviations after surgery (0.58 to 0.88) are large and overlap with the before values, and no sample size is given, so the improvement may not be significant.

questions.question: Calculate the difference that surgery makes to the mean glucose uptake in the non-diabetic group and the type II diabetic group.
questions.answer: Non-diabetic: 0.32 a.u. increase; type II diabetic: 0.70 a.u. increase
steps: Non-diabetic: 1.39 - 1.07 = 0.32 a.u.
Type II diabetic: 1.10 - 0.40 = 0.70 a.u.
Surgery therefore makes more than twice as much difference in the type II group.

questions.question: Which is the function of tRNA in cytokine synthesis (options given in text)?
questions.answer: A identifies an amino acid and transports it to a ribosome
steps: tRNA carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome.
Its anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon during translation.
It does not act as a template for DNA or RNA polymerase, so A is correct.

questions.question: Which organelle chemically modifies cytokine proteins before they are secreted (options: Golgi apparatus, ribosome, smooth ER, vesicle)?
questions.answer: A Golgi apparatus
steps: Proteins made on rough ER are transported to the Golgi apparatus.
The Golgi modifies proteins (for example by adding carbohydrate groups) and packages them into vesicles for secretion.

questions.question: Describe the role of DNA polymerase in DNA replication during cell proliferation.
questions.answer: DNA polymerase joins complementary nucleotides to the 3 end of each new strand by forming phosphodiester bonds.
steps: DNA polymerase binds to each template strand at the replication fork.
It adds free nucleotides that are complementary to the bases on the template strand (A-T, G-C).
It forms phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides, building the new strand in the 5 to 3 direction.

questions.question: Explain how cytokine genes can be expressed in an activated T lymphocyte.
questions.answer: Activation switches on transcription factors that bind the promoter, so RNA polymerase transcribes the gene into mRNA that is translated.
steps: Antigen binding activates the T lymphocyte, switching on specific transcription factors.
These bind to the promoter region of the cytokine gene, allowing RNA polymerase to bind.
RNA polymerase transcribes the gene into pre-mRNA, which is processed and exported from the nucleus.
Ribosomes translate the mRNA into cytokine protein, which is modified and secreted.

questions.question: Explain why different cytokines can activate different cells.
questions.answer: Each cytokine has a specific shape that binds only to receptors on the target cell membrane, so only cells with that receptor respond.
steps: Cytokines are signalling proteins with a specific tertiary structure.
Target cells have membrane receptor proteins with complementary shapes.
Only a cell with the matching receptor binds the cytokine and is activated.
Different cytokines therefore bind different receptors, so T killer cells and B cells are activated separately.

questions.topic: Different CD45 Forms From One Gene
questions.question: Describe how different forms of the CD45 protein can be produced from a single CD45 gene.
questions.answer: Alternative splicing of the pre-mRNA includes or excludes different exons, producing different mRNAs and so different CD45 proteins.
steps: The CD45 gene is transcribed into pre-mRNA containing several exons.
Different exons are included or excluded when the introns are removed (alternative splicing).
Each different mRNA is translated into a different form of the CD45 protein.
Different lymphocytes express different splicing patterns, so their CD45 forms differ.

questions.question: Draw an arrow on the diagram of part of a human kidney to show the location of a single Bowman capsule.
questions.answer: An arrow drawn to point at a spot in the cortex, the lighter outer region of the kidney between the dark outer layer and the medulla pyramids.
steps: Bowman's capsules (with their glomeruli) are microscopic and lie only in the cortex.
So the arrow's head must end in the cortex region, not in the medulla (the darker striped pyramids) or the pelvis.

questions.question: Where in the kidney are most amino acids reabsorbed from the nephron (options: collecting duct, distal tubule, loop of Henle, proximal tubule)?
questions.answer: D proximal tubule
steps: Almost all amino acids and glucose are reabsorbed from the filtrate in the proximal convoluted tubule.
This is done by sodium co-transport and the proximal tubule has many microvilli for this.
The other parts reabsorb only small amounts of amino acids.

questions.question: Which row shows the correct pathway taken by a water molecule through the kidney nephron?
questions.answer: B: glomerulus, proximal tubule, distal tubule, collecting duct
steps: Filtrate forms first at the glomerulus, then flows through the proximal convoluted tubule and, after the loop of Henle, the distal convoluted tubule.
It finishes in the collecting duct, so B is the only row with this order.

questions.topic: Countercurrent Multiplier In Loop Of Henle
questions.question: Explain how the loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier to produce concentrated urine.
questions.answer: The ascending limb pumps Na+ out into the medulla, making it hypertonic, so water leaves the descending limb and the collecting duct draws water out.
steps: The ascending limb is impermeable to water but actively pumps Na+ (and Cl-) out into the medulla.
This makes the interstitial fluid of the medulla very concentrated (hypertonic).
The descending limb is permeable to water, so water leaves it by osmosis into the medulla, concentrating the filtrate further.
Filtrate reaching the collecting duct is more concentrated, so with ADH more water is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated.

questions.question: Describe how ADH is involved in controlling the water potential of the blood.
questions.answer: Low blood water potential is detected by osmoreceptors, which raise ADH release; ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed.
steps: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a fall in blood water potential (rise in solute concentration).
They stimulate the posterior pituitary to release more ADH into the blood.
ADH binds to receptors on collecting duct cells, causing aquaporins to be inserted into the membrane.
More water is reabsorbed by osmosis, so the blood water potential rises and urine becomes more concentrated.

questions.question: How many of four adaptations enable a camel to reduce water loss (concentrated urine; high GFR; long loop of Henle; reduced ADH release)?
questions.answer: C 2
steps: Production of very concentrated urine reduces water loss, so this counts.
A high GFR increases the volume filtered and so tends to increase water loss.
A long loop of Henle sets up a larger medulla gradient, so it counts.
Reduced ADH release produces more dilute urine and more water loss, so it does not count.
Two adaptations reduce water loss, so the answer is C.

questions.topic: Water Use Difference Buffalo And Camel
questions.question: Calculate the difference in the volume of water used in a day by a buffalo and a camel, in dm3 (2 s.f.).
steps: Buffalo: 150 x 697 = 104 550 cm^3 per day = 104.55 dm^3.
Camel: 57 x 850 = 48 450 cm^3 per day = 48.45 dm^3.

questions.topic: No Correlation Between Water Use And Mass
questions.question: Suggest two reasons why there is no correlation between water use and mean mass for the species in the table.
questions.answer: Any two: the species live in different habitats and are adapted differently (camel conserves water, buffalo does not); metabolic rate, diet or surface area to volume ratio differ between species; small sample of only five species.
steps: Water use is already given per kg, so it depends on adaptations, not on body size alone.
Camels are desert animals with a long loop of Henle and concentrated urine, so they use far less water than buffalo despite both being large.
Species also differ in diet, metabolic rate and surface area to volume ratio, and only five species are compared, so no overall pattern shows.

questions.topic: Water Type Effect On Kangaroo Rat Mass
questions.question: Determine the effect of the type of water given on the mean mass of kangaroo rats, using the graph.
questions.answer: Mean mass falls steadily without water (120 g to 115 g in 16 days), but rises with fresh water (to about 121 g); sea water first lowers the mass slightly, then it rises to about 120.5 g.
steps: No water: mass falls steadily with time, losing about 5 g by day 16, because water is lost in urine and breathing and not replaced.
Fresh water: mass dips slightly at first (119.8 g at day 2) then rises to about 121 g, a net gain of about 1 g.
Sea water: mass falls to about 119.2 g at day 4, then recovers to about 120.5 g by day 14 to 16, so it is less effective than fresh water but much better than none.
So giving either water type prevents the loss of mass, and the kangaroo rat copes with salty water by producing very concentrated urine.

questions.question: Explain how the nephrons of the kangaroo rat are able to produce very concentrated urine.
questions.answer: Long loops of Henle create a steep medulla salt gradient, and ADH makes the collecting duct highly permeable to water.
steps: The long loop of Henle sets up a steep salt gradient in the medulla by countercurrent multiplication.
High ADH makes the collecting duct very permeable to water, so water is reabsorbed down this gradient, producing very concentrated urine.

questions.question: Complete the diagram of the Bowman capsule showing its blood supply and label two structures.
questions.answer: A cup-shaped Bowman's capsule drawn round the glomerulus, with its wall labelled and the glomerulus, efferent arteriole or proximal tubule labelled.
steps: Draw a double-walled cup enclosing the capillary knot (glomerulus), with a gap (capsule space) between the capillaries and the outer wall.
Show the capsule wall continuing into the proximal convoluted tubule at one side.
Draw the efferent arteriole leaving the glomerulus (narrower than the labelled afferent arteriole).
Label two of: Bowman's capsule, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, proximal convoluted tubule, podocytes.

questions.question: Which substances are normally filtered from the blood in the Bowman capsule (options: amylose and glucose; glucose and sodium chloride; potassium ions and haemoglobin; urea and prothrombin)?
questions.answer: B glucose and sodium chloride
steps: Ultrafiltration lets small molecules through the capillary wall, while large molecules are retained.
Glucose and sodium chloride are small and are filtered.
Haemoglobin and prothrombin are large plasma or blood proteins and are not filtered; amylose is not in blood.

questions.question: Which row shows the route taken by a water molecule through a nephron in the kidney?
questions.answer: D: proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct
steps: After the glomerulus, filtrate passes through the proximal convoluted tubule, then down and up the loop of Henle, then the distal convoluted tubule, and finally the collecting duct.
Only row D has this order.

questions.question: Describe how glucose reabsorption takes place in the nephron.
questions.answer: Glucose is taken up by sodium co-transport in the proximal tubule, then leaves the cell by facilitated diffusion into the blood.
steps: Na+ is actively pumped out of the proximal tubule cell into the blood by the Na+/K+ pump (using ATP).
This lowers Na+ inside the cell, so Na+ moves in down its gradient with glucose (sodium co-transport) via carrier proteins.
Glucose accumulates inside the cell and leaves across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion into the blood.

questions.question: Which statement describes the production of urea (options: in kidneys from amino acids; in kidneys from glycogen; in liver from amino acids; in liver from glycogen)?
questions.answer: C in the liver from excess amino acids
steps: Urea is made in the liver by the ornithine cycle.
Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver, releasing the amine group used to make urea.
Glycogen is not a source of urea, so C is correct.

questions.question: Which row in the table shows the energy use in muscle contraction?
questions.answer: B: ticks for breaking the cross bridge and removing calcium ions; cross for release of ADP and Pi
steps: ATP binds to the myosin head to break the actin-myosin cross bridge.
ATP provides energy for the calcium pump that actively moves Ca2+ back out of the sarcoplasm.
Release of ADP and Pi is the result of ATP hydrolysis, not a use of the energy, so that column is a cross.

questions.question: Describe the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction.
questions.answer: Myosin heads form cross bridges with actin and pull the thin filaments past the thick filaments, shortening the sarcomere, using ATP.
steps: A nerve impulse releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which binds troponin and moves tropomyosin.
Myosin heads bind to exposed actin binding sites, forming cross bridges.
Myosin heads swivel (power stroke), pulling actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere.
ATP binds to myosin to break the cross bridge and is hydrolysed to re-cock the head; the sarcomere shortens as the filaments slide.

questions.question: State two conclusions about the mean masses of the three ostrich muscles shown in the table.
questions.answer: Zimbabwean Blue ostriches have larger mean mass of each muscle than South African Black ostriches; in both types the muscles rank T > G > F in mass.
steps: For all three muscles the Zimbabwean Blue mean is higher (T 0.88 against 0.69 kg, G 0.74 against 0.59 kg, F 0.50 against 0.40 kg).
Within each type, muscle T has the greatest mean mass, then G, then F, the smallest.

questions.question: Comment on the validity of conclusions drawn from the data for the two ostrich groups.
questions.answer: The conclusions are not very valid because only 2 Zimbabwean Blue ostriches were measured, against 34 South African Black, so the Blue sample is not representative.
steps: n = 2 is far too small to give a reliable mean or to show a real difference, and the unequal sample sizes make comparison weak.
Standard deviations overlap for muscle T (0.69 +/- 0.10 and 0.88 +/- 0.11), so a real difference is not certain there.
Age, sex, diet and rearing conditions are not given or controlled, and no statistical test was done.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage difference in the mean mass of muscle G between the South African Black and Zimbabwean Blue ostriches (2 d.p.). Use percentage difference between a and b = (a - b) / ((a + b) / 2) x 100.
questions.answer: 22.56 % (muscle G is larger in the Zimbabwean Blue ostriches)
steps: Use a = 0.59 and b = 0.74, so a - b = -0.15 and the mean of a and b = (0.59 + 0.74)/2 = 0.665.
Percentage difference = -0.15 / 0.665 x 100 = -22.56 %.
The size of the difference is 22.56 % (2 d.p.).

questions.question: Describe the role of the hypothalamus in maintaining a steady internal temperature.
questions.answer: The hypothalamus receives impulses from thermoreceptors and triggers responses that increase or decrease heat loss and heat production.
steps: Thermoreceptors in the skin and the hypothalamus detect changes in blood or body temperature.
The hypothalamus acts as the thermostat, comparing the temperature with the set point (about 37 degrees C in mammals).
If too hot, it triggers vasodilation and sweating; if too cold, it triggers vasoconstriction, shivering and raised metabolism.
These responses are negative feedback that keeps body temperature steady.

questions.question: Which substances are filtered from the blood in the Bowman capsule of a healthy individual (options: glucose and prothrombin; glucose and urea; glycogen and urea; urea and prothrombin)?
questions.answer: B glucose and urea
steps: Glucose and urea are small molecules that pass through the filter.
Prothrombin and glycogen are large plasma proteins or stored polysaccharide, so they are not filtered.

questions.question: Which part of the Bowman capsule prevents plasma proteins being filtered out of the bloodstream (options: basement membrane; smooth muscle of capillaries; epithelial cells of collecting duct; epithelial cells of loop of Henle)?
questions.answer: A basement membrane
steps: The basement membrane is a mesh of collagen and glycoproteins that acts as a size-selective filter.
Plasma proteins are too large to pass through this mesh and so are retained in the blood.

questions.topic: Glucose Uptake Mechanism In Proximal Tubule
questions.question: Which transport mechanism is responsible for the uptake of glucose into the cells of the proximal tubule (options: endocytosis, exocytosis, osmosis, sodium co-transport)?
questions.answer: D sodium co-transport
steps: Glucose enters proximal tubule cells together with Na+ through carrier proteins.
The Na+ gradient is maintained by the Na+/K+ pump, so the uptake is co-transport.
Osmosis is water movement, and endocytosis and exocytosis move bulk material, so D is correct.

questions.question: Describe how the loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier.
questions.answer: The ascending limb pumps Na+ out, making the medulla hypertonic; water leaves the descending limb, multiplying the gradient along the loop.
steps: Filtrate flows down the descending limb, which is permeable to water, so water leaves by osmosis into the hypertonic medulla.
Filtrate flows up the ascending limb, which is impermeable to water, and Na+ and Cl- are actively pumped out.
Each stage adds to the concentration gradient in the medulla, so the gradient is multiplied along the length of the loop.
This gradient allows water to be reabsorbed from the collecting duct, producing concentrated urine.

questions.question: Calculate the ratio of mean urine production rate for females in the nothing, water and salt solution groups (1 s.f.).
steps: Read the female bars: nothing about 100, water about 840 and salt solution about 440 cm^3 per hour.
To 1 s.f. these are 100 : 800 : 400.
Dividing by 100 gives 1 : 8 : 4.

questions.question: Describe two conclusions from the results of the urine production investigation.
questions.answer: Drinking water gives the highest urine production in both sexes; salt solution gives more urine than nothing but far less than water; with water or salt solution, females produce more urine than males.
steps: Urine production rate was greatest after drinking water (males about 580 and females about 840 cm^3 per hour) and lowest with nothing to drink (about 120 and 100).
Salt solution gave an intermediate rate (males about 210 and females about 440 cm^3 per hour), so the type of drink affects the volume of urine made.
With nothing to drink males made slightly more urine than females, but after water or salt solution females made more, so the response differs between sexes.

questions.topic: Effect Of Drinking Water On Urine Output
questions.question: Explain the effect on the mean urine output of the group that drank water.
questions.answer: Drinking water lowers blood solute concentration, so ADH falls and less water is reabsorbed, giving a higher urine output.
steps: Drinking water dilutes the blood, so its water potential rises.
Osmoreceptors detect this and reduce ADH secretion.
Less ADH means the collecting duct is less permeable, so less water is reabsorbed.
More dilute urine is produced, so the urine output increases.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term mutation.
questions.answer: A change in the base sequence of DNA (genetic material) of an organism.
steps: A mutation is a random change in the base sequence of DNA.
This can be a substitution, deletion or insertion of one or more bases.
It may alter the amino acid sequence of a protein.

questions.question: Name the type of nuclear division taking place as a tumour develops.
questions.answer: Mitosis
steps: A tumour forms when cells divide uncontrollably.
Body cells divide by mitosis, producing genetically identical daughter cells.

questions.question: How many of four statements about epigenetic modification are correct (base sequence change; histone modification; altered phenotype; DNA methylation)?
questions.answer: C 3
steps: Epigenetic modification changes gene expression without changing the base sequence, so statement 1 is false.
Histone modification (e.g. acetylation) and DNA methylation are epigenetic, so statements 2 and 4 are correct.
Altered gene expression can change the phenotype, so statement 3 is correct.
Three statements are correct, so the answer is C.

questions.question: Explain how oestrogen may result in the proliferation of some breast cancer cells.
questions.answer: Oestrogen diffuses into the cell, binds an intracellular receptor that acts as a transcription factor, and switches on genes that promote cell division.
steps: Oestrogen is a lipid-soluble steroid hormone, so it diffuses through the cell membrane.
It binds to a specific receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus, forming a hormone-receptor complex.
The complex acts as a transcription factor, binding to DNA and switching on (up-regulating) genes.
Genes for proteins such as cyclins are expressed, promoting the cell cycle and so proliferation of cancer cells.

questions.question: Suggest how acetylation of histone proteins could result in increased gene expression.
questions.answer: Acetyl groups neutralise the positive charge on histones, so DNA is less tightly bound and genes are more accessible for transcription.
steps: Histones are positively charged proteins that bind tightly to negatively charged DNA.
Adding acetyl groups neutralises this positive charge, so DNA is less tightly wound around the histones.
The DNA is exposed, so transcription factors and RNA polymerase can access the gene and expression increases.

questions.question: Which substances are filtered from the blood in the renal capsule (options: glucose and fibrinogen; glucose, fibrinogen and urea; glucose and urea; urea and prothrombin)?
questions.answer: C glucose and urea
steps: Glucose and urea are small molecules that pass through the filter.
Fibrinogen and prothrombin are large plasma proteins that are retained in the blood.

questions.question: Which structure acts as the filter in the renal capsule (options: basement membrane; cells lining the renal capsule; endothelial cells of capillaries; podocytes)?
questions.answer: A basement membrane
steps: Blood is filtered through the capillary endothelium and the basement membrane.
The basement membrane is the main size-selective filter that holds back large molecules.

questions.topic: Glucose Uptake Into Proximal Tubule Cells
questions.question: Which transport mechanism is responsible for the uptake of glucose into the cells of the wall of the proximal tubule (options: diffusion, endocytosis, sodium co-transport, osmosis)?
questions.answer: C sodium co-transport
steps: Glucose is taken up together with Na+ through carrier proteins (co-transport).
This is driven by the Na+ gradient maintained by the Na+/K+ pump.

questions.question: Explain why some urea is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.
questions.answer: Water is reabsorbed from the proximal tubule, so urea becomes more concentrated in the filtrate and diffuses back into the blood.
steps: Water and many solutes are reabsorbed from the proximal tubule.
This leaves urea more concentrated in the tubule fluid than in the blood.
Urea, a small uncharged molecule, therefore diffuses down its concentration gradient back into the blood.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage decrease in the rate of urine production 10 minutes after the injection (2 d.p.).
steps: Rate at 0 min = 7.0 cm^3 min^-1 and at 10 min = 0.6 cm^3 min^-1, so the decrease is 7.0 - 0.6 = 6.4.
Percentage decrease = 6.4 / 7.0 x 100 = 91.43 % (2 d.p.).

questions.question: At what times should more measurements be taken to find the lowest rate of urine production (options A to D)?
questions.answer: B: at 1-minute intervals between 5 minutes and 15 minutes
steps: The lowest measured rate is 0.6 at 10 min, but the readings at 5 min (1.1) and 15 min (1.0) are both higher, so the true minimum could lie anywhere between 5 and 15 min.
Extra readings must cover this whole range, so B is correct; A and C cover only half of it and D takes repeats at the same times.

questions.topic: Explain Urine Results After Salt Injection
questions.question: Explain the results of the investigation in which salt solution was injected into the carotid artery, using the table.
questions.answer: The salt solution lowers the water potential of the blood, so more ADH is released and the kidney reabsorbs more water, cutting urine production; as the blood returns to normal, ADH falls and urine production recovers.
steps: Injected salt raises the blood solute concentration, so osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the lower water potential.

The posterior pituitary releases more ADH, which makes the collecting duct more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine forms: the rate fell from 7.0 to 0.6 cm^3 min^-1 by 10 min.
Water reabsorption restores blood water potential, so ADH release falls (negative feedback) and urine production rises again, to 2.4 cm^3 min^-1 by 30 min.
Rate is still below the starting value at 30 min, so the blood concentration has not yet fully returned to normal.

questions.question: Calculate the magnification of the photograph of the Bowman capsule, given the diameter from X to Y (standard form).
questions.answer: About 7.4 x 10^5 (x 740 000), using a measured length XY of about 52 mm
steps: Measure the line X to Y on the photograph: about 52 mm (this depends on the measurement, accept about 50 to 54 mm).
Convert to the same unit as the real size: 52 mm = 52 x 10^6 nm = 5.2 x 10^7 nm.
Magnification = image size / real size = 5.2 x 10^7 / 70 = 7.4 x 10^5.

questions.question: Calculate the volume of the spherical Bowman capsule with diameter 70 nm, using V = 4/3 x pi x r^3 (2 s.f., nm3).
steps: Radius = 70 / 2 = 35 nm.
Volume of a sphere = (4/3) x pi x r^3 = (4/3) x pi x 35^3.

questions.question: Which specialised receptor detects changes in plasma solute concentration (options: baroreceptor, chemoreceptor, osmoreceptor, thermoreceptor)?
questions.answer: C osmoreceptor
steps: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in solute concentration (water potential).
Baroreceptors detect pressure, chemoreceptors detect gases and pH, and thermoreceptors detect temperature.

questions.question: Suggest one reason why plasma solute concentration must be kept within a narrow range.
questions.answer: To keep the water potential of the blood constant so cells do not gain or lose water by osmosis.
steps: Cells gain water by osmosis if plasma is too dilute, and may swell or burst.
Cells lose water if plasma is too concentrated, and may shrink.
A narrow range keeps cell volume and enzyme function stable.

questions.topic: Response To Drinking Too Much Water
questions.question: Describe how the body responds when drinking too much water lowers plasma solute concentration and raises blood volume.
questions.answer: Osmoreceptors detect the lower solute level, so ADH falls and more dilute urine is produced; baroreceptors also reduce ADH and aldosterone to restore volume.
steps: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the fall in plasma solute concentration.
Less ADH is released from the posterior pituitary.
The collecting ducts become less permeable, so less water is reabsorbed and more dilute urine is produced.
Stretch receptors detect the higher blood volume, reducing aldosterone and ADH further so the volume falls back to normal.

questions.question: Which method reabsorbs glucose from the proximal convoluted tubule into the blood (options: co-transport with sodium ions, endocytosis, exocytosis, osmosis)?
questions.answer: A co-transport with sodium ions
steps: Glucose is taken up into cells with Na+ by co-transport.
Osmosis is water movement and endocytosis and exocytosis handle bulk material, so A is correct.

questions.question: Calculate the rate of glucose filtration in mg per second if the healthy Bowman capsule filters up to 7.5 g of glucose per hour.
steps: Divide by 3600 seconds in an hour: 7500 / 3600 = 2.08 mg per second.
To 2 s.f. the rate is 2.1 mg s-1.

questions.question: Explain how the kangaroo rat body temperature is regulated to stay between 38.5 and 40 degrees C during exercise.
questions.answer: The hypothalamus detects the rise in temperature and triggers sweating, vasodilation and reduced heat production to lose heat.
steps: Thermoreceptors and the hypothalamus detect the rise in body temperature above the set point.
The hypothalamus triggers vasodilation of arterioles near the skin, increasing heat loss by radiation.
Sweating (or panting, in some mammals) increases evaporative heat loss.
Once temperature falls back, these responses are reduced by negative feedback.

questions.question: Suggest how kangaroo rats are adapted to survive in areas with little drinking water and dry seeds.
questions.answer: Long loops of Henle and high ADH concentrate urine, and water is made by metabolism of seeds.
steps: Kangaroo rat kidneys have long loops of Henle, which produce very concentrated urine.
High ADH levels make the collecting ducts highly permeable to water, reducing water loss.
Metabolic water from the breakdown of dry seeds provides additional water.

questions.topic: Urine Difference Kangaroo Rat And Human
questions.question: Calculate the difference in urine produced over seven days by the kangaroo rat and the human, in standard form.
questions.answer: 1.05 x 10^4 cm^3 (10 497 cm^3) more urine in the human
steps: Kangaroo rat urine = 0.45 cm^3 per day x 7 = 3.15 cm^3.
Human urine = 1500 cm^3 per day x 7 = 10 500 cm^3.
Difference = 10 500 - 3.15 = 10 496.85 cm^3 = 1.05 x 10^4 cm^3 in standard form.

questions.topic: Water Gain And Loss In Kangaroo Rat Versus Human
questions.question: Comment on the differences in water gain and water loss between the kangaroo rat and the human, using the diagram.
questions.answer: The kangaroo rat gains water mainly from metabolism and loses very little in urine, while the human drinks most of its water and loses much more in urine; this fits the rat's adaptation to dry conditions.
steps: Gain: the kangaroo rat gets 1.8 of its 2 cm^3 (90 %) from metabolism, from respiring dry seeds, and takes in no drinking water; the human gets 1500 of 2500 cm^3 (60 %) from drinking and only 10 % from metabolism.
Loss in urine: only 0.45 of 2 cm^3 (about 23 %) in the rat but 1500 of 2500 cm^3 (60 %) in the human, because the rat has long loops of Henle and makes very concentrated urine.
Faeces are small in both (0.09 and 100 cm^3), as the rat's faeces are very dry, so little water is lost there.
Evaporation is 73 % of the rat's loss (1.46 cm^3) against 36 % in the human, as a small animal has a large surface area to volume ratio, but its total loss is still tiny and it balances its gain.
Total water gained equals total lost in each (2 and 2500 cm^3 per day), showing water balance.

questions.topic: Structure Transporting Blood To Renal Vein
questions.question: Which labelled structure on the nephron and blood supply diagram transports blood to the renal vein (options Q, R, S, U)?
questions.answer: A: Q
steps: R is the afferent arteriole bringing blood to the glomerulus, S is the proximal tubule and U is the collecting duct.
Q is the blood vessel (vasa recta) that runs alongside the loop of Henle and carries blood on to the venule and renal vein.

questions.question: Which labelled structures would be found in the medulla region of the kidney?
questions.answer: A: P, Q and U
steps: P is the loop of Henle, Q the vasa recta and U the collecting duct, and all three extend down into the medulla.
R, S and T (afferent arteriole, proximal and distal convoluted tubules) lie in the cortex.

questions.topic: Structures A And B In Proximal Tubule
questions.question: Explain how structures A and B and their locations in the proximal convoluted tubule enable reabsorption of solutes, using the micrograph.
questions.answer: A (microvilli) give a large surface area on the lumen side for absorption, and B (mitochondria) beside the base of the cell supply ATP for active transport of solutes into the blood.
steps: Structure A is the microvilli (brush border) on the side facing the lumen, which greatly increases surface area in contact with the filtrate, so more glucose, amino acids and ions are reabsorbed quickly.
Structure B is the many mitochondria, which make ATP by aerobic respiration.
They lie near the base of the cell, next to the capillaries, supplying ATP for the Na+/K+ pump that keeps the sodium gradient driving co-transport, so solutes are moved efficiently into the blood.

questions.question: Comment on the results of the investigation in which individuals drank 1000 cm3 of water, using the table and graph.
questions.answer: Drinking water raises urine volume and lowers its ion concentration to a peak/trough at 60 minutes, then both return to the starting values by 150 minutes, showing osmoregulation by negative feedback.
steps: Urine volume rose from 100 cm^3 at 0 min to a maximum of 325 cm^3 at 60 min, then fell back to 100 cm^3 by 150 min.

Ion concentration fell from 6.0 to a minimum of 1.8 a.u. at 60 min then rose back to 6.0, so the urine was most dilute when the volume was greatest; total ions (volume x concentration) stayed about 590 to 600, so only water excretion changed.
Mass of urea also peaked at 60 min (about 6.4 a.u., up from 2.0) and then fell back to 2.0 a.u. at 150 min.

Explanation: the extra water lowered the blood solute concentration, so osmoreceptors cut ADH release, collecting duct permeability fell and less water was reabsorbed; as blood concentration returned to normal, ADH rose again and urine returned to its original state.

questions.question: Explain how excessive release of ADH causes the blood sodium concentration to fall in hyponatraemia.
questions.answer: Excess ADH makes the collecting duct very permeable, so too much water is reabsorbed, diluting the blood sodium.
steps: Excess ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water.
More water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the filtrate into the blood.
The blood volume increases and the sodium ion concentration is diluted, so it falls below normal.

questions.question: Which describes the effect of the afferent arteriole being wider than the efferent arteriole (options: increases pressure in glomerulus for ultrafiltration; increases water movement by osmosis; reduces risk of capillary damage; reduces water reabsorption)?
questions.answer: A it increases pressure in the glomerulus for ultrafiltration
steps: A wider afferent arteriole lets more blood in, and the narrower efferent arteriole restricts outflow.
This raises hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus, driving ultrafiltration.

questions.question: How much blood will be filtered in 24 hours if the kidneys filter 6000 cm3 each hour (options: 124 dm3, 144 cm3, 144 dm3, 1440 cm3)?
questions.answer: C 144 dm3
steps: Blood filtered in 24 hours = 6000 cm3 x 24 = 144 000 cm3.
Convert: 144 000 / 1000 = 144 dm3, so C is correct.

questions.question: Calculate the volume of urine produced in one day with an ADH concentration of 75%, assuming ADH stays constant (standard form).
steps: From the table, at 75 % of maximum ADH the rate of urine production is 1.5 cm^3 min^-1.
One day = 24 x 60 = 1440 min, so volume = 1.5 x 1440 = 2160 cm^3.
In standard form this is 2.16 x 10^3 cm^3.

questions.question: Describe the effect of ADH concentration on the concentration of urine and the rate of urine production.
questions.answer: Higher ADH concentration produces more concentrated urine and a lower rate of urine production.
steps: ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water.
More water is reabsorbed, so the urine becomes more concentrated.
Less water remains in the filtrate, so the rate of urine production falls as ADH concentration rises.

questions.topic: ADH And Water Movement From Collecting Duct
questions.question: Explain how ADH affects the movement of water from the lumen of the collecting duct into the blood.
questions.answer: ADH causes aquaporins to be inserted into the collecting duct membrane, so water moves out by osmosis into the hypertonic medulla and then into the blood.
steps: ADH binds to receptors on collecting duct cells, triggering a cAMP second messenger pathway.
Aquaporin water channels are inserted into the cell membrane, increasing its water permeability.
Water moves out of the collecting duct lumen by osmosis into the hypertonic medulla and then into the blood.

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show the molecule formed when the two amino acids join together (dipeptide).
questions.answer: A dipeptide HO-C(=O)-C(R)(H)-N(H)-C(=O)-C(R)(H)-N(H)-H with a peptide bond between the left N and the right C(=O), plus a water molecule H2O.
steps: Remove the OH from the carboxyl group of the right-hand amino acid and one H from the amino group of the left-hand amino acid.
Join the C of the right molecule's carboxyl to the N of the left molecule with a new C-N peptide bond: ...C(R)(H)-N(H)-C(=O)-C(R)(H)-N(H)-H, keeping the free HO-C(=O) at the far left.
Draw the removed OH and H as the second product, water (H2O).

questions.question: Which type of reaction joins two amino acids together (options: condensation, decarboxylation, hydrolysis, phosphorylation)?
questions.answer: A condensation
steps: Two amino acids join with a peptide bond.
A water molecule is removed in the process, which is a condensation reaction.
Hydrolysis is the reverse, breaking the bond by adding water.

questions.question: Describe what happens to the amino acids produced when excess proteins are broken down.
questions.answer: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver: the amine group becomes urea, and the keto acid is respired or converted to glycogen or fat.
steps: Excess amino acids cannot be stored, so they are deaminated in the liver.
The amine group is removed and converted to urea, which is excreted by the kidney.
The remaining keto acid is used in respiration or converted to glucose, glycogen or fat for storage.
